'''Carlo Rinaldini''', or '''Renaldini''' (30 December 1615 – 18 July 1698),{{sfn|Giannini|2016}} was an Italian [[mathematician]], [[military engineer]], [[philosopher]], and [[metrologist]] from [[Ancona]].

==Biography==
Born into an aristocratic family originally from [[Siena]], Rinaldini studied at the [[University of Macerata]] and the [[University of Bologna]]. He was in the service of [[Pope Urban VIII]] and obtained the supervision of the fortresses of [[Ferrara]], [[Bondeno]], and [[Comacchio]] from [[Taddeo Barberini]], the pope's nephew. He also tutored Barberini's children.{{sfn|Giannini|2016}}

Rinaldini was appointed [[rector (academia)|rector]] at the [[University of Pisa]], and subsequently a Professor of Mathematics there from 1649 to 1666. Rinaldini was a friend to [[Galileo]] and [[Giovanni Alfonso Borelli|Borelli]], who nicknamed him "Simplicio" for his fidelity to traditional [[Aristotelianism]].<ref name=Boschiero>{{cite book|first=Luciano|last=Boschiero|chapter=What it meant to be a Cimento academician|title=Experiment and Natural Philosophy in Seventeenth-Century Tuscany: The History of the Accademia del Cimento|series=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science |pages=93–109|volume=21|location=Dordrecht|publisher=Springer|year=2007|doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-6246-9_4|isbn=9781402062452}}</ref>{{rp|98}} Rinaldini corresponded with [[Vincenzo Viviani]]<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Capturing, Modeling, Overseeing, and Making Credible: The Functions of Vision and Visual Material at the Accademia del Cimento|first=Giulia|last=Giannini|year=2023|editor1-last=Valleriani|editor1-first=M|editor2-last=Giannini|editor2-first=G|editor3-last=Giannetto|editor3-first=E|title=Scientific Visual Representations in History|publisher=Springer, Cham|doi=10.1007/978-3-031-11317-8_7|page=227|isbn=978-3-031-11316-1 }}</ref> and with [[Leopoldo de' Medici]].<ref name=Giannini23>{{cite journal|last=Giannini|first=G|year=2023|title=Establishing an experimental agenda at the Accademia del Cimento: Carlo Rinaldini's book lists|journal=Annals of Science|volume=80|issue=2|pages=112–142|doi=10.1080/00033790.2023.2168060|pmid=36680492|hdl=2434/951634|hdl-access=free}}</ref> The correspondence with Leopoldo de' Medici helped establish the experimental agenda for the [[Accademia del Cimento]], which was founded in 1657.<ref name=Giannini23/> Rinaldini was an active member of the Accademia.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Beretta|first=Marco|title=At the Source of Western Science: The Organization of Experimentalism at the Accademia Del Cimento (1657-1667)|journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London|volume=54| 
number=2|year=2000|pages=131–51|doi=10.1098/rsnr.2000.0104 |jstor=531963|pmid=11624506 }}</ref>

As part of the Accademia, he proposed an experiment on the diffusion of heat. When a metal ball was frozen in ice, thermometers below the ball had the highest temperature drop; when a metal ball was heated, thermometers above the ball had the highest temperature rise.<ref name=Boschiero/>{{rp|166}} This disproved the idea that heat and cold propagated in a spherically uniform way, which led physicist and meteorologist W. E. Knowles Middleton to credit Rinaldini with the discovery of [[convection (heat transfer)|convection]] in air.{{sfn|Giannini|2016}}<ref>{{cite book|last=Middleton|first=W.E. Knowles|title=The Experimenters: A Study of The Accademia del Cimento|url=https://archive.org/details/experimentersstu0000midd|url-access=registration|year=1971|publisher=The Johns Hopkins Press|location=Baltimore, MD|isbn=0-8018-1250-X|page=35}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Brush|first=Stephen G|title=The Development of the Kinetic Theory of Gases: VII. Heat Conduction and the Stefan-Boltzmann Law|journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|volume=11|issue=1|year=1973|pages=38–96|doi=10.1007/BF00357437 |jstor=41133371}}</ref>

Rinaldini had numerous disagreements with his friends and with [[Francesco Redi]] and [[Evangelista Torricelli]]. Rinadini opposed the theory, advanced by Redi, that insects can be born from parent plant [[gall]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Emily C|last=Parke|title=Flies from meat and wasps from trees: Reevaluating Francesco Redi's spontaneous generation experiments|journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part C: Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences|volume=45|year=2014|pages=34–42|doi=10.1016/j.shpsc.2013.12.005 |pmid=24509515 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Italian Studies|publisher=Taylor & Francis|title=La retorica dell'esperimento: per una rilettura delle Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti (1668) di Francesco Redi|language=it|first=Corinna|last=Onelli|pages=42–57 | date=16 Feb 2017|volume=72|issue=1|doi=10.1080/00751634.2017.1287254}}</ref> He thus anticipated the hypothesis that [[gall-inducing insect|gall insects]] were born from eggs laid by individuals of the same species, promulgated by [[Malpighi]].<ref name=Redi1>{{cite web archived|url=http://www.francescoredi.it/database/redi/redi.nsf/b4604a8b566ce010c125684d00471e00/3a49786e2a9601acc12569f9003830ba!OpenDocument|archive-date=2006-05-12|url-status=dead|title=Carlo Rinaldini|work=Francesco Redi scienziato e poeta alla corte dei Medici|language=it}}</ref><ref>{{cite web archived|url=http://www.francescoredi.it/Database/redi/redi.nsf/pagine/51CF57B499BA49B6C12569FF0039DFCC?OpenDocument|archive-date=2006-05-09|url-status=dead|title=Lo sviluppo delle ricerche sulle galle|work=Francesco Redi scienziato e poeta alla corte dei Medici|language=it}}</ref>

In 1667, Rinaldini left [[Tuscany]] to go to the [[University of Padua]], where he held the chair of [[Philosophy]] and published ''Philosophia rationalis, atque identità naturalis''. He tried in vain to return to Pisa. He then moved to [[Venice]], where he became the teacher of [[Elena Cornaro Piscopia]], who was the first woman in the world to obtain a [[doctorate|doctoral degree]] when Rinaldini declared her to be a {{lang|la|Magistra et Doctrix Philosophiae}} in 1678.<ref>{{cite book|last=Guernsey|first=Jane Howard|title=The Lady Cornaro: Pride and Prodigy of Venice|url=https://archive.org/details/ladycornaropride00guer|url-access=registration|year=1999|publisher=College Avenue Press|isbn=9781883551445|page=155}}</ref><ref name=WomenBios>{{cite web|accessdate=15 June 2025 |url=https://mathwomen.agnesscott.org/women/piscopia.htm
|title= Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia |first=Sarah |last=Thieling
|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]]}}</ref>

In 1694, Rinaldini was the first person to propose a method for [[thermometer]] calibration using the freezing and boiling points of water as fixed references, dividing the scale into equal [[degree (temperature)|degrees]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Benedict|first=Robert P|title=Fundamentals of Temperature, Pressure, and Flow Measurements|publisher=Wiley|year=1984|pages=4–5|isbn=978-0-471-89383-7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ecSn5SDXDTkC&pg=PA4}}</ref><ref name=Howarth/> [[Christiaan Huygens]] originally suggested using freezing and boiling points as standards in 1665,<ref name=Bolton/>{{rp|45–46}} but scientists were unsure whether those standards would hold across different latitudes.<ref name=Howarth/><ref name=Grodzinsky>{{cite book|last1=Grodzinsky|first1=E|last2=Sund Levander|first2=M|chapter=History of the Thermometer|title=Understanding Fever and Body Temperature|year=2019|pages=23–35|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-21886-7_3|pmc=7120475|isbn=978-3-030-21885-0}}</ref> Rinaldini argued that the ice and boiling temperatures are universal,<ref name=Grodzinsky/> and his scale divided the temperature span into 12 degrees.<ref>{{cite book|last=Schlager|first=Neil|title=Science and Its Times: Understanding the Social Significance of Scientific Discovery|publisher=Gale Group|year=2000|volume=4|page=320|isbn=978-0-787-63936-5}}</ref><ref name=Bolton>{{cite book|title=Evolution of the Thermometer|first=HC|last=Bolton|publisher=Chemical Publishing|location=Easton, Pennsylvania|year=1900|url=https://ia601307.us.archive.org/22/items/evolutionoftherm00boltrich/evolutionoftherm00boltrich.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|56}} Rinaldini's degrees were calibrated by measuring known mixtures of boiling and freezing water, although that method was subsequently found to be unreliable.<ref name=Howarth>{{cite book|first=RJ|last=Howarth|chapter=The Heat of the Earth|page=300|year=2024|title=The Emergence of Geophysics: Journeys into the Twentieth Century|publisher=Geological Society Memoirs|location=London|volume=60|doi=10.1144/M60-2022-32}}</ref><ref name=Bolton/>{{rp|57}}
